title: My Shoulder Popped Out Once — Will It Keep Dislocating?
metaDescription: After a first shoulder dislocation, recurrence is common under 30 and usually appears within two years. Who needs surgery, who does not, and recovery times.
intro: It happens in a moment — a fall on an outstretched arm, a tackle in kabaddi, a dive for a catch — and the arm is suddenly held stiffly against the body with an odd squared-off look to the shoulder. Someone in casualty puts it back, the pain stops almost immediately, and you go home in a sling. The real question arrives a week later, when the shoulder feels nearly normal: is this going to happen again? The answer depends mostly on your age and what you do with your arm.

sections.heading: Will my shoulder dislocate again after the first time?
sections.body:
Quite possibly, and age is the strongest single predictor. In a large US emergency-department study, the highest rate of repeat dislocation — 64% — was in people under 30, and nearly half of all shoulder dislocations happened in the 15-to-29 age group. Over 30, the risk falls substantially.

The reason is structural, not a matter of toughness. When the ball comes forward out of the socket, it commonly tears the labrum — the cartilage rim that deepens the socket — off the front of the glenoid. That injury is called a Bankart lesion. If it heals detached, the shoulder has less to stop it slipping next time, and the next dislocation usually takes less force. The AAOS puts it plainly: once a shoulder has dislocated, it is vulnerable to dislocating again, and repeated episodes are what is meant by chronic shoulder instability.

Timing matters too. Recurrent instability usually declares itself within the first two years. If you are 19 and playing contact sport, that is the window in which you will find out.
bullets: Under 30, male, and playing contact or overhead sport — highest risk group
First dislocation caused by significant trauma, with a torn labrum — higher risk
Bone loss from the socket rim or a dent in the ball — considerably higher risk
Over 30, low-demand activities, no bone loss — much lower risk

sections.heading: What actually gets damaged when a shoulder comes out?
sections.body:
More than it looks from the outside. The front of the capsule and its ligaments are stretched or torn, the labrum is often pulled off the socket rim, and in some cases a piece of bone chips off the socket or a dent is punched into the ball as it levers over the rim.

An X-ray is essential — it confirms the direction of the dislocation and shows any fracture. MRI and CT are usually done later, after the shoulder has been put back, and they are what tell your surgeon whether there is bone loss, which changes the treatment plan entirely.

Two things are genuine emergencies rather than something to watch for a few days. If the hand is cool, pale or has a purple tinge after a dislocation, the blood supply may be injured. If part of the arm is numb or you cannot lift or move it, a nerve may be involved. Either one means the same-day emergency department, not a clinic appointment next week. A shoulder that is still out of joint is also an emergency — it should be reduced under proper sedation, not wrenched back by a bonesetter.

sections.heading: How long should I wear the sling, and does the position matter?
sections.body:
Shorter than most people expect. A meta-analysis found that immobilising the shoulder for longer than one week does not reduce the risk of it dislocating again, and most protocols use a simple sling for roughly one to three weeks.

You may read about slings that hold the arm turned outwards — external rotation bracing — on the theory that this presses the torn labrum back against the socket. The evidence is mixed. Some studies show slightly lower recurrence, including one randomised trial in the 20-to-40 age group; a literature review found no advantage over a standard sling. The braces are also awkward to live with. Worth discussing with your surgeon, not worth insisting on.

The more useful point: a long spell in a sling buys you nothing and costs you stiffness. What the shoulder needs is graded rehabilitation, started once the acute pain settles.

sections.heading: Can physiotherapy alone stop it happening again?
sections.body:
For many people, yes — and it is the right first step for most. The AAOS approach to shoulder instability is nonsurgical treatment first: activity modification, anti-inflammatories for the early pain, and physiotherapy to strengthen the rotator cuff and the muscles controlling the shoulder blade. Several months are often needed before you can judge whether it is working.

That plan works best for the lower-risk shoulder: someone over 30, without bone loss, not returning to contact sport. Rotator cuff strength is not incidental — weakness of the internal and external rotators has been associated with recurrent instability, which is the argument for rehabilitating properly rather than stopping when the pain goes.

Where honesty is required is with the 18-year-old kabaddi or cricket player. Physiotherapy will get that shoulder comfortable and strong, but it does not reattach a torn labrum, and recurrence figures for young athletes treated without surgery are high. Trying rehabilitation first is still a legitimate choice — but it should be a choice made with the numbers in front of you, not a default.

sections.heading: When is surgery genuinely the right call?
sections.body: When the shoulder has dislocated repeatedly, when imaging shows significant bone loss, or when a young athlete would rather not spend the next two years finding out. Surgery is not automatic after one dislocation, and a single episode in a 45-year-old office worker usually does not need it.

table.caption: How the decision is usually approached. This is a general guide — the actual decision depends on your imaging, your sport and your own priorities, and is made with your surgeon.
rows: First dislocation, over 30, no bone loss, non-contact activities
Recurrence risk is substantially lower in this age group
First dislocation, under 25, contact or overhead sport

sections.heading: What does stabilisation surgery involve, and how long is the recovery?
sections.body:
Most stabilisations are done arthroscopically — keyhole. The torn labrum and capsule are reattached to the socket rim with suture anchors; where there is meaningful bone loss, a bone-block procedure such as a Latarjet is used instead. A sling follows, then staged rehabilitation.

The results are worth knowing in numbers. In one randomised study with ten-year follow-up, 62% of first-time dislocations managed conservatively went on to dislocate again, compared with 9% of those repaired. Reported recurrent instability after arthroscopic Bankart repair has been as low as 8.1%, with a pooled failure rate across twelve studies of 13.7%; after a Latarjet, reported recurrence is as low as 0 to 5.4%. Patients typically return to sport somewhere between four and six months after surgery, and most get back to their previous level.

None of that makes surgery risk-free or inevitable. Some stiffness afterwards is common, and the AAOS is clear that the result depends heavily on committing to the physiotherapy — the slow, unglamorous part. Whichever route you take, the shoulder that gets strong is the one that stays in.

faqs.q: Will my shoulder dislocate again after the first time?
faqs.a: Often, if you are young. In a large emergency-department study the highest recurrence rate — 64% — was in people under 30, and nearly half of all shoulder dislocations occurred between ages 15 and 29. Risk falls substantially after 30. Recurrent instability usually shows itself within the first two years after the original injury.

faqs.q: Do I need surgery after one shoulder dislocation?
faqs.a: Usually not straight away. Nonsurgical treatment — a short period in a sling followed by physiotherapy — is the standard first approach, and it works well for people over 30 without bone loss. Surgery is generally advised for repeated dislocations, for significant bone loss, and is worth discussing early for young contact-sport athletes, who have high recurrence rates without it.

faqs.q: How long should I keep my arm in a sling after a dislocated shoulder?
faqs.a: Usually one to three weeks. A meta-analysis found that immobilising for longer than one week does not reduce the risk of the shoulder dislocating again, so a long spell in a sling buys stiffness rather than stability. Slings that hold the arm turned outwards have mixed evidence and no clear advantage over a standard sling.

faqs.q: Can physiotherapy prevent my shoulder from dislocating again?
faqs.a: It can, particularly if you are over 30, have no bone loss and are not returning to contact sport. Strengthening the rotator cuff and shoulder-blade muscles improves control, and weakness of the rotators has been linked to recurrent instability. In young athletes, physiotherapy cannot reattach a torn labrum, and recurrence rates without surgery remain high.

faqs.q: How long after shoulder stabilisation surgery can I play sport again?
faqs.a: Most patients return to sport around four to six months after surgery, and most reach their previous level. Recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart repair has been reported as low as 8.1%, with a pooled failure rate of 13.7% across twelve studies. Some stiffness afterwards is common, and the result depends heavily on completing the rehabilitation.

footerNote: A shoulder that is still out of joint, a cool or pale hand, or numbness in the arm after a dislocation needs the emergency department the same day — not a bonesetter and not a wait-and-watch week. For everything else, an assessment with imaging is what turns guesswork into a plan.
